utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This afternoon we'll begin with a short discussion of what I consider to be an important issue in this case. It relates to the admissibility of some evidence that the Defence has introduced and no doubt will continue to seek to introduce. I set out the matter as follows, and after I have introduced the subject, I'll invite the Defence and then the Prosecutor to make some submissions. The indictment alleges that the accused, as commander of the Bosnian Serb forces conducted a campaign of shelling and sniping upon civilian areas and upon the civilian population in Sarajevo. By virtue of those acts, the accused is charged with the crimes of terror, a violation of the laws or customs of war; murder, a crime against humanity; inhumane acts, a crime against humanity; and unlawful attacks on civilians, a violation of the laws and customs of war. We have heard 13 witnesses for the Defence. Some of them have given testimony which, if believed, would establish that the ABiH committed acts of violence against the Bosnian Serbs which led to suffering on the part of the Bosnian Serbs and even a general state of fear on their part. The question is whether this evidence is admissible. It is admissible if it is relevant and probative. The primary issue is relevance. This evidence appears to answer the charges against the accused by saying that the ABiH also committed acts of violence amounting to crimes against the Bosnian Serbs. Now, I'm not fond the Latin tag "tu quoque," because I do not find it helpful to say that -- or to say simply that tu quoque evidence is inadmissible. That tag masks -- obscures the real issue, which is whether evidence is admissible. Such evidence is not admissible if it is not relevant, and relevance remains the determinant of admissibility. By "relevance" I mean evidence that is probative of the general issue of the guilt or innocence of the accused or of some more specific issue in the case. It is well acknowledged that the concepts of relevance and probative value overlap. See, for example, Cross, a famous author on evidence. He says one fact is not relevant to another if it does not have real probative value with respect to the latter. Applying that to the problem that we face, the evidence from these witnesses will therefore be admissible if it assists the Trial Chamber in determining the general issue of guilt or innocence of the accused or, as I said, of some more specific issue in the case. And I remind everyone that what we have here is a court of law, and we are not running a university course in the history or sociology of the conflict in Sarajevo. The issue is important, because if the Trial Chamber is not satisfied about the relevance of this kind of evidence, then it should be excluded. In some cases this would mean excluding the evidence of a witness in its entirety and in others in some parts. So against that background, I invite first the Defence, Mr. Tapuskovic, to make some brief submissions, having in mind the questions that I posed to you in relation to the evidence of certain witnesses whom we have already heard. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. I understood well the framework you established concerning the scope of my answers in response to the proposition you've expressed, and I'll do my utmost to do it in such a short time. You know very well that as early as our pre-trial brief we stated our basic position to the extent necessary. We never contested the fact that all international humanitarian law is applicable to any and every war. However, we contested all of the core facts of the indictment in spite of a judgement that had been issued before. We believed from the start that it would be necessary for us to refer to the time and circumstances which set a background for all of the things mentioned in the various counts of the indictment. First and foremost, we were aware that we had to deal with things by which a campaign of attacking civilians and civilian facilities was stipulated in the indictment. I can tell you right away that it would be difficult for Defence to bring a single witness that was an eyewitness to many of the things that the indictment is based on, the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic. We might be able to bring one witness who would be able to spoke on one incident. In our belief, we don't even need experts. However, we will bring them here in order to deal with certain aspects of Prosecution evidence, in order to tackle the exemplary cases which were supposed to confirm the facts set out in the indictment and its annexes. It is belief, with all due respect for the Chamber, that such representatives -- such representative events based on the evidence put forth by the Prosecution did not prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. It is something that we believe can be assessed even now at this moment, even without a single piece of evidence on our part being assessed as probative on the part of the Chamber. Therefore, we based our belief that we can deal with the issues from the indictment; although, we were not aware of the entire framework of the things that we had to deal beyond the scope of the indictment. Up until this moment, we don't know what the extent of adjudicated facts will have, the adjudicated facts of the preceding case, and we find ourselves before an insurmountable problem and that is how to choose the witnesses to brought here, since we lack the witnesses who were there at the time and place of the incidents that serve as the basis of this indictment. We short-listed the number of witnesses and documents that would be introduced through those witnesses and in written form, which were not introduced in the Galic case, and here I primarily mean the written evidence on the activities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We could do nothing else but go through each of the Sarajevo municipalities, and they go way beyond Stari Grad, in order to be able to bring, say, two witnesses per municipality to be able to tell you what they went through at the time since there were no other witnesses. The only witnesses are the people who were there and then, and those were the people who took up arms to defend their houses. These were no idle people sporting weapons on certain hills, doing the things that the accused is accused of. Your Honours, if we look at item 5 of the indictment, the part that you, Your Honour, began your introductory remark today, in item 5 it says that there was a campaign of sniping activity and shelling of the civilian population of Sarajevo. In item 7 it is stated that the Serb forces had a dominant view and control of the citizens of the city, as well as they were in the position to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo. In item 13, again we have the mention of the civilian population of Sarajevo. In item 14, the attacks on Sarajevo civilians were deliberate, and so on and so forth. Item 16, attacking civilians. And item 18, sniping and shelling against civilians. The life of virtually of which every Sarajevo inhabitant became a daily struggle, and so on and so forth. And we move on. In almost each and every count there is a mention of civilian population and civilian areas. This goes all the way until the end and only towards the end of the indictment there is a mention of "a conflict." Only after this stage of the proceedings and after all the evidence we saw, our learned friends from the Prosecution say that it is not in dispute that there were combat activities, that there is no dispute about the fact that there was suffering on both sides. It is mentioned only now. However, in the indictment, the entire situation is treated as if there was nothing else but the civilians who were the sole target of those who were opening fire upon them. The entire indictment is set out in a way to show that it was an unprotected civilian setting which comprised no one but civilians. This would have been one of the most serious crimes I have ever heard had it been like that. It could be compared to any great sieges of cities throughout history. However, we are bound to the circumstances and the time relevant to the indictment. As a Defence counsel, it is my only role, first of all, to deal with the problem of the location of Sarajevo, of what Sarajevo is. Is it only the old town, or is it also Grbavica, Hrasno, Nedzarici, and Dobrinja? Is Sarajevo only Hrasnica, or is Sarajevo also Ilidza, Ilijas, Rajlovac, and Vogosca? And to conclude -- or, rather, not to conclude, I am still at the beginning, rather. In item 7, and that is why we brought some witnesses here, and I believe it became clear during the Prosecution case as well, was that this item 7 that insists that the city was besieged and exposed to non-stop artillery and sniping attacks and that the sniping artillery attacks came predominantly from the positions in the hills around Sarajevo from where the attacker had a clear, dominant view of the city and its civilian population. Even during the Prosecution phase of the case -- even during the Prosecution case based on undisputable documents and witness testimony, it was shown that on Mojmilo hill, Strpsko Brdo, Humsko Brdo, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, and so on and so forth that there were Muslim forces there. Therefore, this very important hypothesis of the Prosecutor which managed to survive through the Galic case we believe in -- should be put into question in all its aspects. There are several different aspects to that problem that need to be dealt with in order to see whether the VRS forces were indeed at Spicasta Stijena or at Trebevic and Zlatiste, as well as the Jewish cemetery since these were the only locations from which the Serb forces could act. However, they had no range to reach the city, and which leaves Metalka the only location from which the Serb forces fired throughout the war. The witnesses we've been bringing for you to see are the people from those locations, and they are able to tell you and show you whether one can do any sniping from certain locations and who could have opened fire from certain hills. This is all for you to consider. What we believe is very important is the nature of intermingling parts of the city. We cannot determine who was in the graver situation, whether it was the people in old town or the ones at Nedzarici or in Grbavica or Hrasno or Ilijas or Ilidza or Vogosca. All those micro-locations were set in a way that each of them had difficulties of their own. All this needs to be put in the framework of the indictment and the time relevant to it, between August 1994 until December 1994 and then from December 1994 until May and June 1995 and then up to the end of the war of the. Having considered all this, we have to go through each of the periods and who could have been possible, could have been able to decide to stop the suffering of all Sarajevo inhabitants. We cannot distinguish between those who were in Lukavica and those in old town or those in Hrasnica as opposed to Ilidza or those in Grbavica as opposed to the ones in Ilijas. It is only then that we can assess this statement of the Prosecutor which says that this sole primary goal was to terrorise civilians or, rather, in our view that it was the situation at the time where the suffering on the part of civilians was unavoidable. If we employ the tu quoque principle, we need to deal with the enormous number of civilian casualties in Sarajevo caused by the reckless people who held no regard for the number and type of casualties. There was a great wish on the part of the VRS not to allow to suffer the same fate as was suffered by those who remained in Sarajevo. I do understand your question as to the importance of this, but especially towards the war it was increasingly important to keep your positions and to do nothing else, irrespective of several other aspects that I have been mentioning such as the -- such as history, strategy, and everything else, although some of such aspects may have been present at the outset of the war. In such circumstances, we are able only to bring such witnesses which can testify to the daily life of people in any and every part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand you to say that the primary goal was not to terrorise civilians. You have said "sole," but I think you should say "primary," not "sole," because "primary" is the word used in the indictment. The primary goal was not to terrorise civilians and that suffering on the part of civilians was unavoidable, but the Prosecutor might then say to you, What about the evidence of persons taking up positions in the Metalka building and shooting at civilians in trams or elsewhere and causing injury or death to them? And they might ask the question whether that is not enough evidence of an intent to inflict terror. Again I want to stress that we are not in the stage of closing arguments. I am just exploring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, as I said at first, of course this is no closing argument, but it is our view that not a single incident which is supposed to be a representative sample of what was happening was not proven beyond reasonable doubt. Of course we can discuss the nuances that need to be assessed, of course, at a certain stage so as to be able to determine whether some consequences could have been foreseen and therefore prevented. However, we believe that already on the basis of what -- the things we have as to anything being proven beyond reasonable doubt, it is precisely the Metalka building that was not proven in that case -- in that way, as well as many other incidents encompassed in the indictment. We will try to prove that, or, rather, we will ask you to assess that based on the evidence brought forth up until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- yes. Don't elaborate. I understand the position you're taking. You're saying that on the evidence the Prosecution has not established the sniping and shelling of civilians by the Serb forces. Is there anything else you wish to say, because we could now hear from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I could say at the end is that if the Prosecution really believes that it is not in dispute that there were -- that there was combat and that all suffered, then what remains is that we should listen to what we have until the end so you could hear the people who were in the old town, who lived in other places. We are not going to bring too many more witnesses so that you can see how things proceeded, what happened. And we are not disputing that circumstances of war lead to the things that happened, but we do insist on the time that these incidents that took place that are cited in the indictment, and all of this during the time that Dragomir Milosevic was commander. And of course, all of this is something that we have to see what it looked like when the decision comes about the adjudicated facts. We are deeply convinced, as I said before, that the adjudicated facts cannot be inherited or transferred or applied to a time period that has nothing to do with what preceded it, other than in the most general of things, and that is why we were forced through our witnesses to point out to you some of the most general background things from the beginning of the conflict, which determined many things which followed. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi -- sorry. Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague saw at one point that what I said and was in the transcript has nothing to do with what I actually stated. This is page 8, lines 6 to 10. Perhaps we can listen to that again and then have it retranslated, because it has nothing to do with what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, can you just tell us what it is? I don't think we have the time to -- is it on the page now? No. It's line 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Page 8, line 6. If this is not what you said, then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let us know what your position is on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This changes the meaning entirely of what has been said. Defence counsel would like to check, please. Maybe we could hear it again and translate it again to make sure that the meaning is right. Here we have a string of words, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat it. Just repeat it. Just tell us what you said and we'll have it interpreted now. Mr. Tapuskovic, just tell us what you said so we can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know -- I don't know English, so this is something that my colleague noticed. This is the point. I cannot follow what is said in English. If it was in French I would be able to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is important that you know that the translation -- maybe I should translate it for him. Maybe I should translate the paragraph for him, but the fastest way of proceeding is to correct the translation and make sure it matches with what Mr. Tapuskovic has said. The tu quoque principle is mentioned, and from what I read on the transcript the meaning is totally different from what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is wrong with what I am is suggesting? Let Mr. Tapuskovic now say what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we need enough time. I just need to tell him, let him know what has been translated into English, because it's in English, and I have to tell him where the mistake is. If you give us enough time to do that, then I shall be able to tell him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're making much of this, but let -- take a minute then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did mention the tu quoque and what was written in the transcript, if we're talking about that principle, we should deal with the large number of civilian victims in Sarajevo because of people who were not careful, who did not take care about the number and the type of victims. Please, I did not say anything in that sense, anything like that. I was talking about, and I have to say this now slowly, that the Serb side and that people who stayed in Sarajevo and that we are leading evidence on experienced horrors in Sarajevo itself, and these were victims who had nothing to do with combat actions, and the sense was precisely that and the Serb side in that sense did not respond in any way to what the Serbs were experiencing in the town. But that was one of the main reasons why the Serbs had to take care of this, to protect themselves in their own territories in order for this not to happen to them as well. So the tu quoque principle has nothing to do with that. The tu quoque principle had to do with the fact that the Serb side in the same way that it was experiencing the things that were going on to the people there was allowing itself to do to the people who stayed on the site where the Serbs were living. That is the sense. Perhaps I didn't say that in exactly same words, but I did not say that the victims were victims of people who were not the careful. No. These were the victims of the most horrific crimes. Yes, I have to put it like that now. Which was important as information for those on the other side so that they could, in the last year of the war, preserve whatever it was that they had at that period of time under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Waespi, I'd like you to attend carefully to -- to this. I think I'm coming closer to understanding what the Defence is saying. They are saying that the case that you have presented is not a proper reflection of what happened in Sarajevo and that when one looks at it through the narrow prism of the sniping and shelling incidents that you have presented, you get a completely wrong picture. They are inviting us to look at it more broadly, in the context of a general state of armed conflict, and in that general state of armed conflict, there are acts of violence perpetrated by the ABiH that led to the suffering of Serbs. And in that general state of armed conflict, what the Defence is saying is that it will not be possible for the Trial Chamber to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the primary purpose of the -- of any acts of violence committed by the Serbs was to inflict terror on the civilian population. They're inviting us to say that because it was a general state of armed conflict, and I believe they would want to say that in that situation it is not possible for a Trial Chamber to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt about this particular thing, which is that this particular charge, which is that the Serbs' primary intention, primary purpose, was to inflict a state of terror on the civilian population. I have confined myself to the terror charge, because I believe that is -- that's a very troubling area, and I don't know whether the Defence was extending this argument to the other charges, the crimes against humanity and the other charges. I'm not sure, maybe Mr. Tapuskovic can tell us that later, but certainly I know they are applying it to the charge of terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is correct that the Defence is entitled to put their side of the case and perhaps even their side -- or the Serbian side of background of context. The Prosecution did the same with our expert, Robert Donia, with some of our witnesses Ismet Hadzic who tacked about Dobrinja 92. So I have no problem with that part of the evidence coming in, at least to provide some background as to the armed conflict, to the intensity of the armed conflict. Maybe 1992, but maybe certainly 1995, the May June 1995 offensive by the ABiH. But, Mr. President, the Prosecution's case is indeed that the majority overwhelming majority of the crimes committed inside the territory, the territory under the command and control of the ABiH was committed by the SRK from outside, and it is first the primary duty of the Defence if they want to put the case to distinguish these parts of armed conflict to which we agree having occurred to the incidents, to the shadowed and unshadowed and incidents of a specific date. Mr. President, the Prosecution has been very, very careful in adducing evidence to show for each of these incidents that there was no military target nearby, that there was no battle occurring on at that day. Some witnesses said it was quiet for a specific period of time. I give you the example of the witness who talked about the Simon Bolivar waterline shelling I think 18th of June 1995. The witness was asked, you know, was it quiet and so on. So to exclude what the Defence calls inevitable suffering of civilians. If there was a big battle raging on that day in Dobrinja, centering perhaps on the Simon Bolivar school, of course there could be a bullet or a stray bullets or perhaps even a mortar which was intentionally -- unintentionally fired could have exploded on the Simon Bulevar school. But this did not happen the Prosecution suggests. So first of all, because, Mr. President, these incidents, I think, 27 incidents of sniping and shelling were illustrative of a much broader number. The Defence has got to isolate them and tell us that there was indeed a battle going on, that these targets, the victims, were not victims of intentional, direct, perhaps indiscriminate targeting but unfortunate victims of war. That would be in our submission a good Defence or a proper Defence. But to show to Defence witnesses huge lists of ABiH armory and ammunition they might have used in June, May 1995, just doesn't help in relation to these specific incidents. The second point I wanted to add, Mr. President, is the famous paragraph 7 of the indictment. The Defence is -- is entitled to show through witnesses, perhaps documents, that some of the vantage points they say were in the hands of the ABiH, and I assume their defence will be that from these vantage points the ABiH shot at their own people. Otherwise, I cannot see why a defence argument could be relevant, because from the perspective of the Prosecution, for sniping you indeed need a direct line of sight between the sniper and the victim. I believe we have established it beyond reasonable doubt for all our incidents on the numerous unshadowed incidents of sniping from Spicasta Stijene or the Jewish cemetery or other famous sniping spots. For shelling, Mr. President, Your Honours, you do not need that. You can launch mortars as was done time and again into Sarajevo, the urban part of Sarajevo under ABiH control without looking at the target. So it doesn't matter whether the SRK was sitting on these famous vantage points, but we say, Mr. President, that the most important vantage points and indeed the territory, the controlling territory around the city was -- which was clearly under siege was occupied by the SRK and not by the ABiH. Let me maybe just mention a couple of other points. And I just repeat it. I think I might have said it in the opening that in relation to the indictment period, the Prosecution doesn't say that all the wrong doings were done by the SRK under the command and control of the accused. We admit that people from within the territory, military members of the ABiH or MUP members may have committed war crimes, but again that does not entitle the SRK to do likewise and shoot back and target at civilians. Because we have heard, maybe not today but I think on another day, the defence of necessity. Again, necessity, responding to something, doesn't allow targeting civilians so that's not a defence. Maybe the last point I wanted to make, Mr. President, is the suffering of the Serbs, and I am in fact grateful for that last intervention by the Defence, because perhaps for the first time I realised it more what the Defence means by -- by the sufferings of the Serbs inside the -- inside the territory controlled by the ABiH, because originally I thought the argument by the Defence was because Serbs were suffering inside the confrontation lines their friends and their family, fathers, outside were angry because of that and in response they would retaliate, or retaliation is perhaps even the wrong word, they would fire into the city. That was, I thought, the Defence argument, but today I understood the Defence saying that the suffering of the Serbs inside was so big that it kind of overtook the suffering of the other people inside the confrontation line. At least that's the way I understood the Defence argument. But again, my point is that if some people, and I agree to that, unfortunately suffered, some Serbs, some Croats, some people suffered not because of the SRK actions but because of ABiH or MUP actions, why does that take away of the suffering and the terrorising of the other people inside the confrontation lines, suffering caused by the SRK? It doesn't take anything away, Mr. President. We don't think it's a defence. And it is certainly not a defence, Mr. President, and it's not relevant for the Defence to bring evidence of suffering of people outside the confrontation lines. Why is Hadzici important, suffering of Serbs in Hadzici for the charges in the indictment? We don't see the relevancy. Again, unless the Defence says because people in Hadzici, Serb people in Hadzici were suffering, they fired shells or were sniping into the city. That's the only link I can see, and the way I understand it that's not the way the Defence puts forward its case. That's all I can say. I hope I have answered your questions. I'm ready to -- to answer anything else if you have more issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I don't know whether you have anything to say in reply. Not for more than five -- five minutes. I would be interested to find out, however, whether the general argument that you have presented in relation to terror would also be applicable to the other charges such as crimes against humanity and unlawful attacks and violations of the law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are some nuances here that we could talk about when all of this is over. For example, if we're talking about the notorious air bombs that are talked about here, and of course then we can put the question of -- and now I'm only speaking in notes. So when this is discussed, perhaps, in cases that such means are used, I'm only talking about this, that if it were to be proved that the army of Republika Srpska used something like that then it could have been be aware, the person who was doing this, that civilian casualties could be the result. I'm just mentioning an example. And we will come to that on condition it is proved who and if anyone used air bombs. Now I'm only talking about it as something that we can discuss if this becomes necessary. However, when we're talking about crimes directly against civilians, for that you would need to have an order, and this is something that the court of first instance did in the Galic case. I'm not going to go back to that. One of the Judges provided a very valuable opinion regarding those orders in that case. So this is a different topic that deserves to be dealt with at some other point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Don't say any more about that. Are you finished now? Well, let us conclude. I thank both parties for their submissions. The submissions were useful in part, but I don't think they were directly to the -- to the question which has been troubling the Chamber for some time, and that is the relevance, the admissibility of the evidence. The Chamber has heard the submissions, and we take them into account. We'll continue to monitor the evidence of witnesses in the same way that we have monitored the evidence of all witnesses in the case, and we will determine on an individual basis the admissibility of evidence on the basis of the accepted criteria of relevance and probative value. Let us have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we just wanted to deal with a procedural issue. We announced that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my colleague Ms. Isailovic will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. This might be a procedural issue, but -- which is based on substance. This has to do with the witness testimonies of the Defence, and the Defence would like to see the names of these witnesses on the 65 ter list. We would like these witnesses to testify under the same conditions as Prosecution witnesses. Pursuant to Rule 21(4)(e) of the Statute. Article 21 of the Statute of this Tribunal. The Defence benefits from what seems to be fewer resources than the Prosecution, because we are two to a team. We have two assistants, one of whom must be present in the courtroom at all times and print out all the documents, whereas the Prosecution does not have to do this. We are understaffed if we compare our position to that of the Prosecution. We have accepted these harsh working conditions, conditions which we have accepted, and we have kept our promises, but we would like to be assisted by the Chamber. We have turned to the Registrar of this Tribunal, which is the easiest way of proceeding as far as we are concerned and returned to the registry to be assisted as regards the witness testimonies of our witnesses. Now, let me explain. During the pre-trial defence conference, Your Honour, you invited us to look into other ways of providing evidence in order to cut down on the Defence time, time which had been allotted to the Defence to present its case. And the case had looked into various other possibilities, and we had planned to do away with some witnesses, but we would like to hear nine witnesses whom we feel are particularly important to the Defence case, but pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It so happens that the Defence team has only two Defence counsel. We are at all times present in the courtroom, and we need to prepare these testimonies in writing beforehand. These testimonies need to be signed by the witnesses. We have asked to be helped by the Registry, but for the time being we have been -- we are hanging out to dry, so to speak, and we are faced with a rather serious problem as things stand today, because we need help from the Registry. We need to be able to use these witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the specific help that you seek?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we asked to be able to use the office of the ICTY in Sarajevo. More specifically, in order to be able to meet up with seven witnesses. We have specified on what dates and what time, two hours per witness, and we have asked to have a printer, because I shall take charge of this. I've got a portable computer, but I don't have a portable printer so that I can take this with me to Sarajevo. And we felt that this was a very reasonable request to use the premises there, and we got a harsh response; it is not for the Registry to look after this. As the Defence was not quite sure of the fairness of this answer, we felt that this was an unreasonable response, and to meet your requirements, i.e., another way of presenting our evidence through our witnesses, we are turning to you today, and we would like to say that those witnesses already on the 65 ter list that have already been approved by the Bench, if we are to spend only three days on this because we can't spend time than that, we need this kind of help. And we feel that this is quite a reasonable request, and we do hope to get it from the Registry of this Tribunal. And let me repeat, pursuant to Article 21, paragraph 4(e) provides for evidence adduced by the Defence under the same conditions as evidence adduced by the Prosecution, and this is the request we put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Isailovic, can I ask a question for clarification? Are you asking the Chamber to order the Prosecution to make available for you -- the Registry or the Prosecution, to make available to you a room in the OTP building in Sarajevo and a printer for the purpose of taking you witnesses there and to extract a statement from them under Rule 92 bis? Is that what you're asking us to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge Harhoff. I should also like to add that we would like to be assisted by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, because we intend to cut down on our costs, because instead of bringing our witnesses to The Hague, we will ask them to come to Sarajevo and Belgrade given that most of these people live in Sarajevo. The Defence does not have any premises in which it could ask these witnesses come to. So we would just like Article 21, paragraph (4)(e) to be abided by, Article of the Statute of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not a hundred per cent sure who owns these ICTY facilities in Sarajevo, but I know for a fact that there is indeed a representative from the VW down there, which is certainly not OTP, and there are some other facilities, and even OTP, although I, you know, cannot give sort of a binding commitment, but I'm sure we could make available a printer, an office down there. That could certainly be accommodated from our perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's very heartening to hear. It may be that the problem can be solved in this way, and I certainly thank Mr. Waespi for that invention. But what I should say is that we have heard the submissions that have been made, and we treat it as -- as a motion. We are not in a position to give a ruling on it now. We need to consider it. Obviously we'll have to look at all the ramifications. We also have to look at the case law of the Tribunal in this matter. But if the problem can be resolved informally, in the manner suggested by Mr. Waespi, then that would be the best -- best solution. So we leave it there, Ms. Isailovic. Be in touch with the Prosecutor. See what help you can get. In the meantime, the Chamber will, in the exercise of its functions, prepare a response to the motion that you have made. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness T-7, you remain subject to the declaration that you made yesterday. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we dealt with the photograph at the end of the day. Could we have the photograph placed before you again, please. This was DD003969. You explained this photograph yesterday. Could you clarify, please, once again? Where did you dig trenches, looking at this ridge? What is it called this ridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's called Ablakovina, and I dug behind that ridge, about 30 metres behind that ridge. From the spot where I dug, the distance to the Serbian positions was just as long if not longer on the road leading towards Pale where the Serbian army was or the road leading to Mount Jahorina where the Olimpik facilities were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you this yesterday. Who made this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I made the photograph after the war when I returned to live in Sarajevo. It was then that I made this photograph for the Galic trial, but it was not included in the evidence and I just happened to take it with me now, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, in the street where you lived at the time of the conflict, was there something going on that you could testify about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made this photograph in order to make it plain to the Court that in these streets which are quite steep and face the slopes of Mount Trebevic, the Muslim forces positioned a car there and attached a mortar to the car. Sometimes they would attach an anti-air machine-gun and that they would shoot from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's easier, again, if first -- the question was very, very broad, and that -- which is part of the problem. If the time-frame would be cleared right now. That's also relevant for the issue of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the period you're dealing with here, Witness, month, year -- or year first and month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from 1993 to the moment when I left I eyewitnessed such events. Whenever there was parliamentary delegation coming, new journalists, new cameramen, in order to illustrate what the situation was in town during the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said from 1993 to the moment that you left. At what time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I object to the relevancy of this evidence if it's an observation sometime before the month of June 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, we have an objection as to the relevance of this evidence as occurring in the pre-indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I still do not know the scope of adjudicated facts in June of 1994. We can ask the witness about this period of time, about the circumstances at the time. However, let's have this photograph and this evidence admitted into evidence, because it is very important in order to establish the situation in the summer of 1994. This witness said it was in June. This is very important to portray how things unfolded in Sarajevo at the time given the circumstances. This is something that this witness could testify about. I think that the events of June of 1994 are very important. These are the things that happened just before this witness left Sarajevo. At any rate, shooting from mortars and other weapons, from cars and trucks is something that is quite important in order to grasp the events in Sarajevo, also during the time covered by this witness, all the way up to June 1994. This is very important in order to comprehend the events in Sarajevo. We cannot say that it is irrelevant, especially given the fact that we also have to analyse to some degree the events which preceded the period of time for which Dragomir Milosevic is charged. This is a very important fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we are going to rule that it is relevant essentially because the indictment period begins the 10th of August, and this is June. So it's June 1994, it's just two months away. But I'm a bit troubled by the argument that Mr. Tapuskovic has raised, and not for the first time, about the pending nature of the adjudicated facts, and I'd like to hear both of you on this point, because that argument would only be valid, it seems to me, if you can show that the Prosecution had made an application for a certain fact to be treated as adjudicated and that it relates to this very -- very issue that the witness is speaking about, and that issue is spending before the Appeals Chamber, and therefore you need to lead evidence on it because don't know the status. Otherwise, I don't see that it is open to you generally to say that this may relate to an adjudicated fact and the issue is pending before the Appeals Chamber. That can't be a general response, I think. I don't see how that could be correct. So we are going to rule the evidence relevant and allow the question to be answered, but I just wanted to hear you on that particular question, Mr. Waespi, on the adjudicated fact argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe that in Galic the issue of mobile mortars played also a role, but it also can only be relevant in this case if there was an adjudicated fact, as you rightly point out Mr. President, that says that there was indiscriminate or any type of shelling into that area where the witness says there was a mortar, ABiH mortar, placed. So that would play against the argument that the SRK would have been shelling this area, you know, indiscriminately, rather than actually being a legitimate military target although it's probably gone when the truck is removed. So only in that sense. If there is a linkage between, as you rightly point out, Mr. President, a specific adjudicated facts to which the Defence is entitled to adduce evidence; only on these circumstances would the Defence argument be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, very briefly on that point, the adjudicated fact point, because we are allowing the evidence but not on that ground, on the ground that it is relevant. What do you mean by referring to the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When referring to adjudicated facts, I am referring to a number of facts contained in the trial judgement, which simply cannot be transferred to the period of time for which Mr. Milosevic is charged. That period of time is only relevant where in light of his action, his responsibility, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But do have in mind one, a particular adjudicated fact, that relates to this -- to the issues raised by this evidence? Because you can't be at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just wait a second, so I can consult my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please look at the fact 173 and then a whole number of facts following it which link these type of events with terror of civilians, intimidation of civilians. There are a number of facts for the period between 1992 and 1994. The Prosecution wants all of them to be admitted as uncontested facts. These are the facts that I was referring to. We were able to find them quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's very good of you. You're much better than I am because I don't have them here. We will proceed, but I'm really interested in the principle. We have said that we will allow the evidence because it is relevant. Whether it's -- it's to be allowed on the basis of the adjudicated fact argument is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, now we have admitted this photograph into evidence, but I need to understand better what it really shows; so therefore, I would like to put a number of questions relating to this photo. First of all, which area of Sarajevo is it really taken from, and what is the direction that we are looking? We're looking up on some hills from somewhere, but where is that and in which direction are we looking? That's the first question. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The photograph was taken from the centre of the town looking from the bridge of Gavrilo Princip facing Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I would prefer to hear it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] See, here, I don't know how familiar you are with the town. On the right-hand side, my right side, is the military barracks of General Kukanjac, and then on the other side is the centre of the town. This is the spot from which the took the picture facing Mount Trebevic, because I wanted to show that it was a steep street in the direction of Mount Trebevic from where the bullets were fired on Serbian positions. And if you want me, I can elaborate on why this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No thank you, but what is the direction that we're looking by compass? Are we looking towards the north, or the north-east or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is south-east. East is this way, so this is south-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we're looking south-east, in the direction of south-east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, imagine this, that you and I would be walking up the hill that you can see on the photograph where there is snow. If we walk in a straight line up, then we would come to the ridge where you have made some red and blue markings. And 30 metres behind that ridge you say there were trenches. Whose trenches were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I dug trenches for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I was resident of that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. And then you told us that a little further on, if we were to continue our walk, then we would stumble on the Serbian trenches; is that correct? What would the distance be between the two lines of trenches at this particular point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I told you, some 30 metres. I dug in several locations, and the closest they were, the two armies, was in that location, except for the Jewish cemetery which is an urban area, and they were positioned there in two buildings facing each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, on the photo you have put a blue spot on top of the peak that is behind this ridge. It's further up and further away. What -- what would we find on top of that peak where the blue point is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to say. I really don't know what is located there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking because I thought -- I'm asking because I thought that this was a separate mark that you had put there to say that. But could you then tell us who held the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I think it's just a natural feature of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Who held that area where the blue point is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This point is above the Serbian positions but high above them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. I understand you to say that it was held by the SRK. Is that correct? That the area behind the region, on top of the next peak where the blue point is, that area was held by the Romanija-Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely so. Everything above the road was held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We must adjourn now for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We seem to have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The interpreters have a technical problem. Has that problem been resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It seems so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in addition to what you already stated as regards the headquarters in your street, there was another command there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Across from the military command there was the headquarters of the 1st Mountain Brigade commanded by a certain Zulic. So in Bistrik there were two mountain brigades, the 1st and the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Musan Topalovic, aka Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was happening there? You mentioned the mortars in the direction of the hill. As for the commands in your street, did they open fire in any other directions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that the fire from those mortars created a lot of unrest or displeasure among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've already touched upon that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some inter-Muslim conflicts. I felt in my apartment when the Grbica school mortar would go off. Musan Topalovic's brigade was there. I followed that grenade, that shell, which landed on the quarters of the special forces of Dragan Vikic that were in another part of town. There were inter-Muslim clashes over territory in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you see that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About twice since I was often digging trenches outside the city. I saw that happen twice while I was in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're on the subject of your street, what else was happening with the inhabitants there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I mentioned inter-Muslim clashes, the most pronounced one was when Alija Izetbegovic, the Supreme Commander, tried to rein in Musan Topalovic, Caco, and his brigade. At least that's what the official justification was. And he was attacked in his own apartment. A police team was dispatched to arrest him, while at the same time Caco's units were blocked on the slopes. In that courtyard which was shared by apartment as well, I saw that 8 out of 10 policemen were captured, and they killed his personal security detail by shots in the head. Later on, we were taken down as hostage, all the people from the building, and then there was crying because there were children there and women, and someone had asked for a knife. Then we were told to stand in a circle, and the remaining two policemen were then killed. They slit their throats and made us watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did something like that happen to the civilians, too, the people who lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caco was the most notorious of Alija's commanders. There were a number of them who were pre-war criminals. Caco was particularly connected to the suffering of the Serbs. It is well-known that he would take individuals and entire families to certain pits in the city, and he wouldn't kill them by bullets. As he himself said it was expensive to spend a bullet on a Serbian life, and he used to kill them in other ways.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer. The interpreter failed to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Would you repeat the end of answer that you just gave. The interpreter wasn't able to get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess it referred to the part where people were being slaughtered at the Kazamati [phoen] location, the pits, because they didn't want to spend bullets on killing them. He slaughtered them during the night and shots would have revealed his position. He feared that the Serb positions could be opened -- that the fire could be opened from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this photograph. I still believe it hasn't been -- you decided to accept it, but I don't remember it having been assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you're saying is, of course, very serious, but were you an eyewitness of these throat-slitting events you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And not only myself. All of the inhabitants of the four surrounding buildings were eyewitnesses to that. Caco made all of us go down to the yard as hostages. And in the conversation with Mr. Izetbegovic, he said he would kill us all if Alija Izetbegovic persisted on taking him in. We were all made to watch. We were ordered to watch. My wife did not want to. She turned her back on the entire scene, and I covered her but watching that I almost fainted. I dream about that even today. I remember that as the gravest of moments of this war for me. A lot of us watched that. It is well-known in Sarajevo. We provided statements before the court as did others. It is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was searched for by Alija Izetbegovic; is that correct? I just wanted to know whether Caco was searched for himself by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Izetbegovic is the late Bosnian president. It was on his orders that the army and the police went there to arrest him and to have a change in command. They had something against Mr. Caco because of his conduct, and I guess there was some other political reasons in the background that I'm not familiar with. However, they must have had their reasons to try and deal with Caco by using a number of troops and policemen; although, Caco had almost 4.000 troops under him. As we know, Caco was killed later that night, and his soldiers were tried after the war. It was in the press that they admitted to killing some 800 people, that group, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what it was that you were able to observe in town? Did you move about, and what could you see personally, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the few in Sarajevo who had both a work and a war obligation, so to say. I was with a state institute for 15 days every month and the other 15 days were spent digging trenches for two years. I saw and went through a lot. An interesting thing that my -- that I might say here is that once it was night, at the beginning of the war soldiers and police would come out onto the streets and the town was plundered, ravaged in a very short time. Therefore, having such commanders around who organised troops was the main reason of concern in -- for the life in the city, because they were plundering. They were not only stealing from the city, but they were also stealing from their own people. They would go into apartments and houses and ask people to collect gold and foreign currency for the needs of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and people gave, and several times at that. Later on they realised that there wasn't much use of doing that. And the citizens complained to the mayor saying that much was taken from them without much effect, and he gave a statement to the press. He was asked when the situation would improve and when the war would stop and the city be freed. He said, On that day and at that moment when the last citizen of Sarajevo has given his last dollar. It is a very concrete statement depicting the overall atmosphere in the city. They were just looking around and trying to spot places to plunder rather than fight the war. And then there was trading on both sides. The Muslim side had some Serbs captured, and on the other side the Serbs had food, drinks, and cigarettes, and then there was trade. One packet of cigarettes for one Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The narrative has been long enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what it was that you saw concerning civilians. Were you able to observe anything regarding the army and weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I went to dig trenches I could on occasion see the schools where the Motorised Brigades were quartered, and I could see the weaponry they had, and I could see their weaponry in much of their positions where I was forced to dig. There were troops and weapons there. I saw several tanks in town, several mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you see the tanks in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Ciglane, the brick factory close to the Kosevo stadium. There was a tunnel. They were inside it, one or two of them, and the other two were across the road in a park of the construction and civil engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your worst fear once out in the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs in Sarajevo were afraid both in their apartments and on the street. Anyone could come to your apartment without knocking. They would barge in, and they always found whatever it was they were looking for, although such a thing never existed in that apartment prior to their arrival. They would simply plant a bullet or a handgun or a bomb, and then they would tell the host that it was found in the apartment. One of them would plant it and another would find it, so to say. And then they would take away such a person or the entire family, and they would go missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about in the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even worse. One would always get stopped and asked for his or her ID, every bridge, every square. And I since they could recognise us by the last name, as is customary in Bosnia, people would be taken away and would disappear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Could you please repeat the end of your answer for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a mention of sniping, but it hasn't been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note, that is the part of the answer that we did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last thing we have you as saying is, "And as is customary in Bosnia, people would be taken away and would disappear." What came after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. What I said was that we could tell each other by our last names, and when the ID cards were checked at the check-points, people were taken away. Some just disappeared. People just simply disappeared. And the worst of it was that after that the person who was watching would give a sign to a sniper somewhere on a high-rise building, and then the person would be followed and later would be shot at or wounded. So this is something that happened on a regular basis. I'm a sportsman, an athlete, so I say that sometimes you could see the snipers walking in threes with their weapons and it looked like Sarajevo was hosting a firing-range championship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I asked you if you were an eyewitness of any of these events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. On the bridge in Novo Sarajevo, New Sarajevo, across from the radio television Sarajevo I was coming back and then I could see that there was a check under way there, and I stopped and those people who were checking the IDs stood a little bit apart, and I could hear them repeating, "Blue shirt. Yes, yes blue shirt." I didn't know what this was about, and then when I passed, I could hear the blue shirt being shot and it was some person called Savo Smth [phoen] Who was wearing a blue shirt, and he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you get by? Did they check your ID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I passed through, but I really have to say that sometime just before the war I bought a car from a friend and his father. I kept the ID. He was a Croat. His name was Ivan Sabic, so I put my photograph in this ID document, so I would cross with no problems. Later when there was a war between Muslims and Croats, I put my own photograph back because it was easier to be a Serb in Sarajevo at the time than a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us how long you stayed in Sarajevo and when you left it? When I say Sarajevo, I mean that part that was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of June. Yes, on the 9th of June, 1994, I crossed. The situation was already quiet. In 1994 there was already cooperation between the two sides, so it was possible to go for two-day visits on either side. So I used that opportunity to cross over, and then I stayed on my side. What can I say? What I saw, I saw. The consequences of war. Every building bore the traces of shots. On the streets I could see defence walls, and I could see tunnels being broken through -- through a whole line of buildings in order to avoid going along the road. There was also a memorial spot from Grbavica where there was a crossing at the faculty of electrical engineering. Everywhere you could see curtains from sheets placed every 20 metres or so that the citizens could protect themselves from snipers and also that cars would be able to pass along there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with you? What were you doing in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately I started to teach at the faculty of electrical engineering, and I worked there until late September, and then from October to December, for three months I spent that time on the front line, on the road. That I talked about earlier and about which His Honour the Judge says that that was until the -- until 1994. But actually, I say that that road and the lines were there until the end of the war. They didn't move. So as I said, I was at the line for three months, and one of the Serb army commanders asked everybody, all those who were on work duty, professors, lecturers, workers from the Energoinvest company to replace the army of Republika Srpska on the lines for a certain period of time because on Mount Treskavica there was still major fighting going on between the Muslim and the Serb armies. So I stayed there for three months, and I can say that I was there with my colleague who also was on a spot that was exposed up there, but I can say that throughout that time we actually spent the time playing chess, and there wasn't really that much to do. It was quiet, and that was fortunate for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you state there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then after that, in December I became the dean of the sports faculty in Pale, and I wasn't exposed to any kind of combat or any kind of war experiences. After that, all I remember is that there was a weapons depot that was bombed by NATO forces, and that was perhaps 400 metres as the crow flies away from my university building. I know everything was shaking and it was quite a powerful explosion that shook us all up. It was quite unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that we could look at another photograph and then finish with that? That is photograph -- actually, a set of four photographs, DD003970. I think that this is the fourth photograph in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can show the photograph on the ELMO. It will go faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who took this photograph, and what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the photograph immediately after the war. I took the photograph from the side from which I was digging. These are Serb houses. I wanted to show how that looked on the other side, because everybody is claiming that one side is shooting and the other side wasn't. The building on the right side is a building in the Beogradska Street that the Muslim forces captured Ljubljanska Street as well as Beogradska Street. That's the building, and they did manage to reach Beogradska Street from Ljubljanska Street and there was a gas explosion in the building so the building broke in two. In one part there were Serbs and the other part there were Muslims, so I would come there from one side to do something -- to do some work and the Muslim forces would say the Serb forces were on the second floor walking around and the Muslim forces were in the basement on the first floor. I just took it so I would show the circumstances. And also from the other side depicting Serb building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this photograph, I would like it to be admitted into evidence, and I am finished with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not admit the sealed document DD03978, and this document relates to the identity of the witness. Could please this document please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it, yes. We admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D242 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you. It shouldn't take that long.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will gladly answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, the commander you mentioned that told you to replace some of the VRS on the front lines for a certain period do you remember -- and I think that it relates to the time you were in Grbavica, from October to December 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am not able to remember either the name or the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember what unit he commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a tall, dark-haired man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And what unit did he belong to? What military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just going back to a point you talked about, that's the -- when you crossed or you were at a bridge in Novo Sarajevo, and you said that there was some incident involving a blue shirt, I guess a person wearing a blue shirt. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be wrong if I mentioned any date. Perhaps I could just go by the season. All I can say is that it was autumn, but I really don't know the day or the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which year was -- would that be, 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know the name of that person who was concerned in this incident, the person who was a victim as you say, the person who I guess wore the blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did state name. Savo. That's what I heard. Later I heard that a certain Savo was killed, and he was wearing a blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you didn't learn that on the spot that he was killed. Somebody else told you later that this person was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we left we heard that there was some kind of shuffle and that you could sense that there was a sniper and everybody fled. And I know that this happened on the bridge or just across the bridge that he was hit, but nobody was hanging around. Later I heard that that person that was there was a person by the name of Savo and Savo is a Serbian name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So did you see that person with the blue shirt yourself there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to another brief topic, and that is the issue of Caco, the famous Caco who was, I understand, taken out by the Supreme Commander, shall we say, Alija Izetbegovic. When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed -- I don't want to get it wrong. I think it was around the 20th of October, 1993. I cannot give you the exact date, but I think it's more or less than -- that's the night that he was killed. He was taken to the Main Staff and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And he was, I believe you testified along these lines, the commander of one of the Muslim brigades. I think it was the 10th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it from your evidence he was a troublemaker and his commander decided to eliminate him. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The last subject is related to the picture we saw at the end of your evidence that was a destroyed building. Now, there was a lot of destruction in -- in the old town in late summer and fall of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The lines of separation, I didn't really see that other than the Jewish cemetery section towards the Serb side where some buildings were damaged, but I claim that out of a hundred mosques not a single one was destroyed or shelled, and there was no question of any demolition of the old town. There were no grenades or shells of such force that could make that sort of damage. Perhaps a building roof would be damaged or the window glass would shatter. That was the sort of damage, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at a couple of -- of pictures. If turn number 03171 could be retrieved, please. And while that's being done, do you know the mosque, because you talked about mosques, of Kobilja Glava? Do you know that mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kobilja Glava. I know that there was Zulfikarpasic mosque on Kobilja Glava. I know that there was a mosque at Kobilja Glava, and if it did, this is outside the town. So I wouldn't necessarily know about it, but I know that in the town of Sarajevo itself out of a 100 mosques none of them were destroyed or suffered serious shell impact. I know that in my apartment there is a hole. That is the kind of more serious damage that was inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, the Kobilja Glava mosque was in the --?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said for the sake of truth the mosque next to me was damaged with a hole, and the transcript states "my apartment."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. There was really a hole on the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you only know about the mosques which were in the centre of your town as you say. You don't know what happened to other mosques like Kobilja Glava, which was near the Kosevo stadium, not too far away from the centre? So you don't know what happened to these mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything in Sarajevo, including those 100 mosques, actually 95 per cent of those buildings were located in the old town or in the centre. I wouldn't really know much about the other parts of the town. I really didn't venture out of Old Town too much other than when I was taken for digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at the building which is centred in the Old Town, I suggest. Do you see what this picture represents? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that that would be the town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, it's the old post in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right. You're correct, the old post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That looks fairly damaged, does it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Look, it wasn't really damaged. None of the walls were damaged. It was burned. The building just burned, but it wasn't knocked down or damaged. All the walls are still standing. I know that because I passed by a hundred times during the war. It looked exactly like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
