utterances.text: Yes. So you agree with me that this is a fairly unusable building, an old symbol. A symbol of Sarajevo was made unusable rather by shells or firing incendiary rounds doesn't matter. It was rendered unusable. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree in the same way that none of the buildings in the Serb side could be used. They all looked just like this one. Any high-rise building, any tall building that was shelled, burned, and looked exactly like that, but none of them had their walls damaged, and now they've all been restored and everything looks very nice. None of them had to be knocked down in order to build a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So when you say that nothing really happened to the Old Town, you mean it all looked like that? It was burned down, it was unusable, but the walls were still standing. That's what you accept that happened to the Old Town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wouldn't put it like that, because from the location where my apartment was, other than the places that were covered by nylon sheets, all the buildings throughout the war had their brick walls exposed. The brick was exposed. That's what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at another instance of a building which you might say is still in great shape, the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next picture could be shown, please. Just the next page of the same sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the library, the old library?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I lived very close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the state of the library in July, August 1992? Do you agree with me that it was shelled from outside the city it, that it burned, and that it's in a horrific -- it was in a horrific state in summer of 1992? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it was in a horrific state, and I deplore damage to cultural buildings. It was in the same condition as the post office, but I watched the building when it was burning, and when I watched I was in a lot of doubt, when I saw flames from the second floor. And I'm not quite sure who could have done that. Was it the Serb side or was it perhaps from the inside. I cannot be sure, but the indications would seem to point to something quite different, because if something is burning from the inside, and I could see the flames from the building, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're suggesting today that the Muslim forces, whoever was inside the confrontation line, they destroyed their own library, their own national library, a symbol of pride? That was done by the inhabitants of Sarajevo, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did not say that. All I am saying is that some true expert investigation may show that what you stated could actually have happened, but, yes, I was also in the bread line in Miskinina Street. It just was fortunate that I wasn't killed or wounded. But with quite a lot of arguments, I could claim that it was a shell that was fired on one's own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And whether --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had time to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did this incident at Miskinina Street happen, the bread line incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23rd of May. It was right at the beginning of the war, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Mr. President, if these two -- or these two photos. It's in fact I think a three-page exhibit could be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P774, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're just in time either to re-examine if you wish or to make a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put just one question to the witness while we still have this photograph on the screen in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was said here that books burned, Muslim books burned. It was a library. Whose library was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose cultural heritage was contained in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it all burned. I have some information that all of that was actually removed in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which books were not removed perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-7 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't answer which books were and which books weren't. I think that not all of it burned and that was what was meant to be removed was removed, but I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness T, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My pleasure. [The witness withdrew].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the next witness is, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next witness is Predrag Carkic. He has no protective measures. T-8, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you please give us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Predrag Carkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 30th of November, 1963?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to finish my question before answering. And you were born in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you've been living in Sarajevo -- or, rather, you lived in Sarajevo in the neighbourhood called Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was your family house where you lived?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary school and your secondary school, technical secondary school, in 1984; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You worked in Energoinvest? I started making mistakes myself. You have to wait for my entire question to be recorded in the transcript before answering. So you worked in Energoinvest in Pofalici; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to show you a map on the monitor, and let us try to cover the questions related to the map as quickly as possible. This is 2872 under 65 ter. Could we zoom in on the northern part, please. Can you read the names of the streets?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Barely. I can't really see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about now?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point to the street where your family house was located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark it with a letter C.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where is the company where you worked? Could you please point to that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please very briefly tell me -- or, rather, tell the Court what happened in early 1992 to you and you were family.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: We lived in the neighbourhood of Pofalici. Humska Street, 145B was the address. Everything was normal up until the month of March, when a member of the wedding party was killed in the Old Town. From that time on, we had guards, night guards. We made arrangements with our Muslim neighbours since there were no Croats living there, to stand guard together in order to avoid any problems or preempt any problems. That's how it was up until the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Court this, you are referring from March, April, up until May. What about these guards? Did people standing guard, be it Serbs or Muslims, have weapons?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Some did. Not all of us had weapons. Mostly we had to trust each other. Some Serbs had weapons as did some Muslims, and the rest of us didn't. So we would go together to stand guard and then if a Serb had a weapon then a Muslim didn't, and vice versa. That was the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you occasionally carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: When the member of a wedding party was killed in the Old Town, some of us Serbs from Pofalici at our own initiative headed towards the intersection by the secondary school for economic technicians in order to make a protest there. When we arrived there, our people from the TO gave us weapons, and this is when I had a weapon myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that people stood guard until what time, without there being a conflict?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There was no conflict up until the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: That's when the first attack came. Most likely the Muslim forces tested positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. In the preceding period of time did something happen to your family?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the 2nd May up until perhaps the 10th of May women, children, and the infirm were taken out of the city through Zuc towards Rajlovac, and then from Rajlovac we went to Tvrdimici and then onwards to Pale. It wasn't just the case with may family. Other neighbours of ours, Serbs, did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many people departed via Zuc and other places?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Definitely 200 or 300 people, if not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what period of time you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Right now I was referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of May until the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The Muslims attacked our neighbourhood. The combat lasted for about half an hour, and then everything went into a lull. In the morning on the 16th there was an all-out attack on Pofalici from all a directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this evidence on the grounds of relevance. This is -- some background is all right and I let this -- I did not rise for a while, but we're now getting into fairly detailed day-by-day, blow-by-blow accounts from the middle of May 1992, 26 or 27 months before our indictment opens, and I submit that the evidence is not relevant to rebutting any of the charges that are laid in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours; Mr. President, I was about to ask the witness what he experienced on the 15th of May. It is relevant because based on document I received on Friday from the Prosecution, on that day about 63 people were killed in the presence of this witness. I have received a document whose translation will be complete in a couple of days. The witness knows the people who were killed on that day. He was captured himself and taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevancy is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Tell us what the relevancy is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevancy lies in the fact that the suffering inflicted during those several days actually led to this terrible situation in the very beginning of the events in 1992. This is what was fatal for the rest of the conflict. On that day alone, 65 people were killed based on the documents we have, based on the documents that the Prosecution has. When I wanted to hear from the witness what he had experienced on that day, whether he was wounded, whether he was taken to the prison, and generally what happened to him, including that he was an eyewitness to the death of a large number of victims, some of whom he knew, which traumatised him for the rest of the life. And this is what marked that period until the end of the war. This was one of the most important events for inspiring fear and was relevant to all of the events which took place until the end of the war, and this is contrary to the claims of the Prosecution that that was the Yugoslav People's Army that was there. No. It was unarmed civilians who were there and who were killed. This is one of the eyewitnesses, perhaps the only eyewitness that I can bring before this Court who can confirm about what had happened on at that day, what happened to him, whom he saw, whom he was able to recognise among the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we are not going to allow this piece of evidence. We find that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not going to allow this piece of evidence. We find that it is not relevant. If you have evidence from this witness which relates to the indictment period or fairly near to it but not 27 months away, then you can lead that evidence from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness confirms that paragraph 7 of the indictment is not something that is tenable. If you look at paragraph 7 -- or count 7 of the indictment then you can see what I'm talking about, why is this not tenable; that these positions were established on the 7th of April, 1992. These positions were taken all the way up until 1995 with a lot of victims. What this witness is supposed to show is that it is not true on that on the 7th of April these positions were formed, or before then. But what he's going to say is that the gravest and most difficult combat took place in May in Pofalici, and it went all the way up until September and that's when the positions were established and the hills taken. This shows that this paragraph of the indictment, paragraph 7 of the indictment, which is very important, shows just how untenable this is, that the hills were taken before April of 1992. This is the essence in a way of the indictment, and this witness is supposed to show that the combat aimed at taking the hills took place much later and that a lot of people were killed in one day alone during that combat. So what this witness has to say is radically different from this item of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have evidence that relates to that part of the indictment, paragraph 7, and I read it: "Even before this date armed forces supporting the Serbian Democratic Party and elements of the JNA, including units of the 4th Corps of the 2nd Military District, occupied strategic positions in and around Sarajevo," if you have evidence from this witness which relates to that, then you can lead it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask him. I want to hear from him. He spoke of May. The entire population of that neighbourhood crossed over to the other side, and I want to know what happened to the people who remained there with a rifle. He himself had a rifle, and he should tell us about what happened to him when on the 15th of May he found himself there with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I would object to that, Mr. President. In fact, I do object to that. I understand the Court's ruling to be that the witness can testify about matters which relate to paragraph 7 of the indictment and paragraph 7 of the indictment does not have anything to do with what happened to this witness if he remained in Pofalici following the events of the middle of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must following the ruling that I made. If the witness has evidence concerning the question of who occupied strategic positions in and around Sarajevo even before the 7th of April, 1992, then you can lead that evidence from the witness. That's my ruling, so follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me who occupied those positions at the time you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There was no one at the position except for us, the civilians. And on -- on Hum, Hum hill, there was the police. There were no troops, no soldiers. Up until that day we were together with our neighbours the Muslims. We had an agreement to stay together at night so as to avoid any conflicts and problems. There were no soldiers or paramilitaries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did soldiers appear?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Their soldiers appeared on the 16th. The Patriotic League, the Green Berets, the special forces of the MUP and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what followed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The 16th of the morning they attacked from the direction of Velesici and Buca Potok as well as the tobacco factory on Drinska Street. They attacked from all directions. The fight lasted for about two or three hours and then everything fell silent. Since I had a rifle I came back home to fetch some ammunition and there was no one there. My father was missing. My neighbour was missing. So I returned to the local commune building in Pofalici and there was no one there, not even the people that I had left there. They all fled. I started moving towards the forest at Zuc hill, and at the foot of it, towards Buca Potok, the Muslim soldiers were there. Then I returned to the house of Zoran Bakic that was on fire, as were many other houses in Pofalici. I hid since two armed men passed by, and I hid in that burning house. There was an old house of a certain Janko Cangalo there next to that one. There was an old bus there, and I hid underneath it and awaited night-time. I tried to pull out twice during the night but I could not. In the morning on the 17th around 6.00 a.m., five Muslim soldiers came towards the bus where they found me and took me prisoner. I managed to gather from their accent that they came from the Sandzak region. One of them took out a knife and hit me on the head with the butt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. This does not relate to the direction that I gave. Does he have any evidence about who occupied those strategic positions in and around Sarajevo? That's what I want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment where were you? Can you tell us? This place where you lived, where you were, what was it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: It was my home. There were no soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. You said it was an elevation.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No. My house was at the foot of Hum hill. The police were up on the hill and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The Muslim police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Until the 16th, when we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How about the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Not a single soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did they attack?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I guess because we were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who took up position at that elevation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which other elevations?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Pofalici Brdo, Hum, and then they moved towards Zuc after I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he say what month this was? No, no, what month? What month of the year is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for how long did the Muslim forces occupy the Hum elevation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Until the end -- when you say throughout the war, what do you mean? Until what year? Let's be specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until end 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that you were attacked. Were you armed? "You" meaning civilians who were there. Did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of us. As I said a moment ago, about a dozen of people had rifles. The others did not. I did, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were there -- was there any crossfire? Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, until the 15th and the 16th when there was the fighting in Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there was shooting as late as that, what happened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: They captured me, and as we were passing by Mr. Neno Pikula's house I was at gunpoint, I saw a terrible scene in front of that house. Dozens of my neighbours were there like sardines, one next to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I don't mean to rise and interrupt so often, but I feel I have no alternative but to object to what I see as the continuing elicitation of irrelevant evidence. And the Court has made clear that this witness's evidence in pre-indictment period is to be limited to the indictment and this scene awful and heart-rending as it is, I do not see as relevant, I do not see as within the Court's ruling, and I object to it being elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that it can be as fine tuned as you have put it. If the incident is -- is related or has some relationship to the occupation of the strategic positions, then it may be scene as -- as relevant. What else do you want to find out, Mr. Tapuskovic, about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This specific incident speaks about the fact that inter alia this position and the hill and the place where this man resided in the course of those few days, all those strategic positions in the north of that part controlled by the army of Herzegovina, including Hum, Zuc, Oric and all other strategic locations in the territory as well as Grdonj were taken over in May and that item 7 of the indictment is incorrect; that the strategic positions were taken up before the 7th of April. That is one thing. Another thing is that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied those and that from the north between -- or starting from the 15th and the 16th, the entire northern part throughout the war, as the witness said, was in the hands of the soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the entire northern slope of the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I consider it relevant, Mr. Docherty, for this reason: That it helps to make more credible Mr. Tapuskovic's case that the hills were occupied by the -- by the Muslims, and it is that occupation of the hills by the Muslims that enabled them to exercise this dominance over the Serbs and to -- indeed to inflict violence on them. So from that point of view I -- I consider it to be relevant. It's time for the break, though, and so we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we save this map, please, and I wish to tender it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, what happened to you after you were pierced with a knife? As you said, you were hurt in your left upper arm.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: When I was captured by the Muslim forces and as we passed by Neno Pikula's house, I saw dozens upon dozens of my neighbours who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where did these Muslim forces come from, the forces who captured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by their accent, I was pretty sure they came from Sandzak. Muslims from Sandzak who came to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether any of them came from the hills which they occupied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an attack on Pofalici that day. They came down from Hum hill, from the direction of Velesici, Buca Potok, and from the direction of Drinska Street and the tobacco factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Tapuskovic, you're bent on one thing. I'm trying to assist your case. That is what makes it relevant, that they came down from Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, please explain from which directions the Muslim forces arrived. As you said, they came from the direction of Hum. Do you know what had taken place a few days prior to that, or did you only follow the events of the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Only the 15th and the 16th. They probably -- the Muslim police had occupied Hum hill, because there was a transmitter there not far from my house. They occupied that position and denied access to everyone. On that day, the 16th when we were attacked, they came from the direction of Hum, Velesici --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where Velesici is, as well as Buca Potok, on the map?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Hum Hill, Velesici. From the direction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate arrows from all of those places towards your house?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the distance between Hum hill and your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About one kilometre to the tower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I'm repeating this for the second time. Next to Neno Pikula's house they were lined up like sardines, one next to the other. And they led me from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you recognise any of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Two. In that confusion and fear I recognised two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The late Zoran Ignjatovic and the late Radovan Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on Friday I received this document from the Prosecution, DD003799. We're going to have to keep the map before I show the document, so perhaps we can save and tender the map as a Defence exhibit with the markings of the witness on the map with the arrows indicating the directions from which the units that captured the place where he lived had come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D245, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at DD003799, which I received at my request only on Friday from the Prosecution, and the translation of which is going to be finished, according to information that I have, in four days' time. So until Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, last Wednesday the Defence asked us for some documents that were given to the Prosecutor while she was on a mission in Banja Luka. We were able to get all of those documents and give them to the Defence on Friday within 48 hours. There was no time to translate documents. The document which Mr. Tapuskovic has just called for is 20 -- 19 or 20 single-spaced pages, all of it in Cyrillic alphabet, B/C/S. Although we gave it to them because it was at their request, we do not have a translation. I do not know what this document says. I have not been able to take a look at it in English, and therefore I have serious reservations about its being used. The Defence, as I say, asked for this document six days ago, and as I say, we were able to get it to them, but we have not been provided with a translation, and yet counsel is wanting to use it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have to use it through this witness, Mr. Tapuskovic, or can it be used through another witness who will testify later, by which time you would have had it translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I'm not going to have another witness with such experiences at Pofalici. He has just said that he recognised among the victims two persons, and he gave their names, and those two persons are here on this list, and I would like to show you pages 4 and 8 in B/C/S. This is already on the e-court, and for the witness to be able to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us know the -- show us the heading of the document. Is it a list of names? The document, is it a list of names?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a list of names with explanations. And then on the following page -- actually, on the third page, before the names, there is information about the substance of the document, and the witness can confirm that. And then these two persons are on the list of victims, and the witness recognised the bodies of these persons as he was passing by them on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Here is what we will do. Show us the information that will tell us where the document came from. That is information about its provenance. And then you can show us the particular passages. They're short, then they can be translated; but we must have enough information to tell us what the document is about. If the Prosecutor is embarrassed by this in the sense that he wouldn't have had enough time to cross-examine properly, I'll take that into account, and it may very well be that I will allow him to ask further questions of this witness at another time. That will be very regrettable. So let us proceed that way. First let us see the information on the document that tells us about its provenance. Let us see the heading and have that translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one day ago, yesterday, we completed the examination of a witness who was not protected, that is Dukic Branislav. Then we showed the Court the document which was admitted into evidence from which it can be seen that these documents were presented to the Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte, they years ago. At our request we received this document relating to Pofalici and Dobrinja. We received it. And then from this document, which we managed to receive from the Prosecution at our request the other day, quite properly I believe that the document concerning Pofalici, and if the Prosecution also has the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not listening to what I'm saying. I'm trying to assist you. The Prosecutor has a perfectly good point. The document is not translated. It is 19, 20 pages. So ordinarily I would simply disallow you, but I'm trying to find a mechanism, a way to have you use the document now, and I outlined what that mechanism is. It is a way that will provide us with information to make the document sufficiently intelligible to us so that we can understand it and so that the Prosecutor can ask questions about it. And the first stage in this process must be what is there in the document that tells us what it is, and who prepared it and when it was prepared? Is there anything in the document that gives that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document from which it can be seen how the document came about, and the document was tendered with Witness Dukic, I can find that document, because the document that was presented to the Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte was accompanied by this material relating to Pofalici and the victims at Pofalici. This document bears the Prosecution numbers, and on page 3 you can see what it's about. The document was prepared by the association from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Republika Srpska, which was tendered through Witness Dukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, that information I am seeking is on another document, not this one? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document DD -- if we can look at Document DD0003786 that we presented yesterday and which was admitted as our exhibit, first we can look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this document was translated. And this is that document, Your Honours. Under Article 11 you can see Sarajevo, and then you can see Pofalici first. And based on that document, we asked the Prosecution for the accompanying documents to this document, and that's when we received this document, Pofalici, which we then introduced into the e-court under number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the number that you just said? The interpreter didn't hear it. You said you introduced it into the e-court under number...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD0003786. 3786. And that document is in front of you. It was introduced or admitted as Exhibit D238. This is Exhibit D238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it signed? Is it signed by anybody, this document we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document -- the document was signed by Madam Carla Del Ponte attesting that she received the accompanying material in May 2004, and then this document is part of the accompanying collection of documents which I would like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know it is signed by Mrs. Del Ponte to show that she received it, but what I was asking was, Was the document itself signed, say, by the person who prepared it? It may not have been. I just want to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no signature here, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think -- does the witness know anything about the association that prepared it? The Association of Prisoners of War of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can ask the witness if he knows anything about the work of this association and the compiling of documents necessary for their work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know President Dukic and the Vice-president Jovicic, nicknamed Slavoj [phoen]. I know the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did they take any information from you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So this document prepared by the Association of Prisoners of War of Republika Srpska sets out the evidence of crimes committed against Serbs, and it was given, it says, to Ms. Carla Del Ponte by the delegation of the association on the 31st of May, 2004, in Banja Luka. So move now to the document which you have and to the names that you wish to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can show the witness page 3 of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the witness to read only the paragraph in front of the first name that is mentioned here. Can you please read allowed this passage.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: "After armed attacks on the 16th of May, 1992, by the military and police units of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the capture of the settlement of Gornji Pofalici, in an attack on an undefended column of Serbian citizens numbering about 3.000 men, women, children, and the elderly, and organised terror on the Serb population which remained in the settlement the following persons were killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 4. It should be page 9, so let's go to the next page. Next page. Page 4 and then we need to look at paragraph 9. Do you see the name next to paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see this man, Buha?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Near the house of Neno Pikula, killed and bent over. I guess he tried to run away or something, so he was basically slumped over a fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page and paragraph 24. You mentioned that name earlier. Where did you see that person?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Across the street when I was speaking earlier how they were lined up like sardines. Among them was also the late Zoka Ignjatovic. He was lying there dead. His legs were -- his leg was wounded. Parts of the leg were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are going to get the translation in a few days. I would like to have this document tendered just for identification with an identification number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just for these paragraphs that have been read out, or do you -- or are you seeking the admission of -- just for these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll mark just these paragraphs as D246.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness could also have looked at the end of the document to see the total number of victims on the list. It's the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the last person on the list and what's the number?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Number 65, Ranko Sojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just this, Your Honours. Could we mark this for identification as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. It's been suggested that we mark the entire document for identification. When we come to deal with the admission, then we will deal with the admission of the specific parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, could we now hurry up in order to complete this as soon as possible? What happened to you afterwards? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers pushed me in the car that is known as Kedi in our area, and then across a hill called Ham [phoen] they took me to Velesici. They beat me there for an hour and held me in house near a mosque, and from there they took me to the central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you in the central prison and how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I remained there for 12 days. On the 17th when I was brought there to the main prison, the first thing they did is they took iron bars and wooden sticks and beat me with it. There was some glass on the -- shattered glass on the ground, and a soldier kicked it with his boot and then put it all in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then what happened after 12 days?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: We were exchanged on the 28th of May at the Vrbanja bridge. They exchanged 25 of us for 25 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which dates it was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: It was on the 28th of May that I was exchanged. From Tilava a neighbour took me to Pale to see my son whom I basically hadn't seen, my wife, and my wife's sister, and my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join any army?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I did after two days. I went to Grbavica again, and I joined the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were your positions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: At Grbavica. From the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge as it was then Miljacka to Strojorad and from Strojorad to the stadium of Zeleznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The entire war, until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What happened to your mouth when the shattered glass was put in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to the glass, they also put salt in my mouth and it hurt my mouth badly. They also put salt in my eyes. On that day, I watched as they killed an older man called Gavrilovic with iron bars. He used to work as a doorman. I went later to the doctor's, and the doctor told me that I was fortunate that they put salt into my mouth because it acted as disinfectant. However, I lost all my teeth due to all the beating. It's such a terrible trauma that I cannot live with it. Even to this day when I go back I feel very uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. That's the story now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, His Honour Judge Robinson asked you about the glass. Did something happen to your mouth?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was blood pouring out of my mouth. And when the Muslim soldier saw that, he poured salt into my mouth. He started cursing my Serbian mother, and he said that the blood wasn't salty enough, and he had to put salt into my mouth because of that. And then after several minutes he started pouring a beer into my mouth and then proceeded to beat me with iron bars and wooden sticks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a terrible story, and you have our sympathy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A true one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's one the worst stories I've heard in my eight and a half years here. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that part of the witness's story, but nevertheless, I would like to hear about the positions where you were. What did you do there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary soldier. After all the traumas I experienced, the ones that I described to you, I didn't want to allow for this to happen to me or to anyone else ever again. This is why I defended the front line, the positions. I told you where the line went. I was just an ordinary soldier there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do there as an ordinary soldier? What was your task?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Just to defend the front line, to ensure that what happened to me on the 16th of May, 1992, would not happen again. Children were being born if Grbavica. There were a lot of unprotected people there. Soldiers from the federation were shooting at me, and I was shooting back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please, we need to cut this short, but tell, me do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the substance, the importance of this witness's evidence, which really is the evidence that he has given about the location of the Muslim soldiers in the hills and that they came from there to -- from those hills to attack him and his neighbours. We are very sorry about what happened to you. That's really the significance of the evidence. I don't know whether you need to carry it on any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just another matter. This witness eyewitnessed another event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell it us, do you remember the period from March or December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this event? What is this event? Does it in any way relate to the paragraph 7 of the indictment. I'm trying to get you to concentrate on the important aspects of your case, Mr. Tapuskovic. Does in it in any way relate to the points that you very properly made about paragraph 7 and in relation to which I have allowed you to lead evidence from this witness? If it doesn't, I'm not going to allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I have completed with that topic. I would like the witness to clarify some other matters concerning the period of time when Dragomir Milosevic was the commander of SRK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we've exhausted the other topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're now moving to the time when the accused was the commander of SRK. Let us hear what you want from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First if you could tell us something about 1994 when you were involved in the conflict, when you were at the positions. Tell us something about what you did there.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't perhaps until October that the fierce attacks of Muslim forces began. We defended Grbavica, and from time to time we went to a place called Kijevo. We had our positions there as well. There were frontal attacks coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when was it the calmest?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an event that you remember in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: On a lovely sunny March day, it was the 11th of March, 1995, it was a day that will never be erased from my mind as long as I live. We sat in Grbavica. It was peaceful, quiet. There were five of us soldiers sitting at the table drinking coffee, and then in front of us less than a metre away there were a couple of girls playing hopscotch; and then all of a sudden we heard a couple of shots and the two girls fell dead right in front of us. We fell to the ground as well, and later on we pulled those girls out. Their names were Lalovic and Ucur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Right near them. The sniper didn't fire at us but, rather, at the girls who were right there playing hopscotch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just a few questions. My name is John Docherty. I'm one of the prosecuting attorneys on this case. You served in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from when and until when, beginning and ending dates if you could, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of June, 1992, until the end of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you've given some testimony it today about events at the beginning of the armed conflict. Who was the first commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I think it was Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there anyone before General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Tomislav Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know then that Tomislav Sipcic was a regular career officer in the Yugoslav People's Army and the first commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Can you answer out loud, please, sir? It's for the benefit of the court reporter who needs to put down what's heard.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General Galic, who you do know, was also a regular career officer in the Yugoslavian People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I know that from the 1st of June, 1992, when I joined the army of Republika Srpska I just know about the army of Republika Srpska. There was no longer any JNA at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about the commanding officer of the corps in which you served, and you've identified General Galic as the 1st Corps commander that you remember, and the question I asked you whether you know that General Galic was a career officer in the Yugoslav People's Army before becoming commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, 1992, I became a soldier of Republika Srpska, and I had never heard of Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about him during your service with the corps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I had the person who was superior to me, my platoon and my company, and there was no other need for me to know anything else. I saw my battalion commander only once and that was on television too. There was no need for me to see him, and I had no occasion to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's go at this a little different way then, sir. During the time that you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the corps had -- I'll just -- I'll just list some standard military equipment, and I'll ask you to say "yes" or "no" according to whether the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had these things. Radios.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Most likely they did, but I can't confirm that since I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: In my area, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What about in other areas?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: My area was between the bridge of Bratsiva-Jedinstva and up to Strojorad and the stadium and there were no pieces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I wasn't clear. I meant to ask you were you aware of there being pieces in other areas?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And without going through a long list of military equipment, isn't it correct that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had equipment from the Yugoslav People's Army? That that's where the SRK's equipment came from?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The JNA took away all of their equipment. What they left were old inoperable pieces, and our people did our best to fix them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is it not correct that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is the 4th Corps of the 2nd Military District of the Yugoslavian People's Army under a new name?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you were not aware of General Galic's career before he became your corps commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you did not recognise the name of General Sipcic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You -- in your own words, "most likely the SRK had radios." You can't confirm that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You suppose that there were artillery pieces in areas other than the area where you were stationed, but you don't know that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I know only about my area. There were no artillery pieces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in your area throughout your time with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps you served as a private soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You did not command other troops, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were not a member of the corps staff at the Lukavica barracks, were you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There was no need for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If there were orders issued by General Milosevic to snipers in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is not something you would personally know about, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so the answer is no, you would not know about orders he might have issued to snipers or to mortar companies or to artillery units within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That's not something that you have personal knowledge of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, in 1992 your testimony is that Muslim forces had control of Zuc and Hum hills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And your testimony is that these were Sandzak Muslims and not Muslims from Bosnia itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: They were mixed. At the moment of my capture those people happened to be from Sandzak. As for the whereabouts of my Muslim neighbours, well, I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But you testified also that earlier, before these very bad events, you and your Muslim neighbours took turns mounting what I'll call a neighbourhood guard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: We were together until the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Relations were good, is that correct, until then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the hills. Sarajevo sits in -- I'll call it the bottom of a bowl, and the upper part of the bowl is formed by the mountains that ring the city; is that correct? And again, sir, I just have to ask you to answer out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Both Zuc and Hum are within that ring of hills, aren't they? They are within the city of Sarajevo itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not. Zuc Hill and Hum Hill are part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So the hills that surround the city and which look down on the city also look down on Zuc and Hum, don't they? I'm just trying to get the geography straight at this point, sir.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You're not certain. Okay. And in any event, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be fair to ask of the witness which are those hills that are higher than Zuc and Hum, otherwise the question posed is not defined clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I'm trying to establish is that there are hills surrounding the city that look down on the city, and I don't think it necessary to go into particular names, and in fact I think it would be misleading because we would have to start at one point right around the clock with a list of names. I think the general point can stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But aren't you also trying to establish that there are hills that look down on Zuc and Hum?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. And what I'm saying is I don't believe that we need the names of those hills. I'm talking about the general geography of the Sarajevo valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think -- let the witness just say. Do you know the names of the hills that look down on Zuc and Hum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is Trebevic, although I don't know about the view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your testimony, sir, was that during 1992, when Pofalici was attacked, that the attacking forces came down from Zuc and Hum hills; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You also testified that they came from the tobacco factory. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that would not involve coming down a hill; is that correct, to get to Pofalici from the tobacco factory, it's all on the same. Do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The place that was attacked by the Muslim's units is below Zuc and Hum Hill and below the altitude of the Velesici settlement and we were besieged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I understand that, but what I'm trying to clear up is this business of coming down hills. Some of the forces came down hills, attacking forces, some of them did not; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you did in the give evidence concerning control of other strategic points within the city of Sarajevo such as bridges, crossroads, important buildings, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in fact, during the time in Pofalici the combat was at fairly close quarters; is that correct? There were attackers and defenders on the same level at close range; correct? You look puzzled. Is the question unclear? I can try again.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'll try again. The actual fighting within Pofalici was between attackers and defenders who were at close range and at the same level, the same altitude, the same height, what have you. Do you understand? Is that more helpful?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There was no fighting in Pofalici until that very day, the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And on the 16th of May 1992, the fighting was at close range between opposing forces that were at the same level.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you -- the part that you disagree with be the close range or the relative altitudes?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: The altitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the fighting, however, was at close range; is that correct? You agree with that portion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just tell us why you wouldn't agree that it was at the same level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Zuc Hill and Hum Hill, well, we were below both. Those Muslim units were higher up, whereas we were below. The Muslims were up there on those elevations, and the settlement of Pofalici is below in a depression. They controlled the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you give testimony when Mr. Tapuskovic was asking you questions about those forces coming down the hill? I remember you drawing the arrows on the map and telling the Bench that it was a distance of about a kilometre. The forces came down the hill to Pofalici; correct? And Pofalici is where the fighting occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Later on in the armed conflict, during the time that General Milosevic was the corps commander, you were a soldier in Grbavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And there are several tall buildings in Grbavica, are there not? There's the --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, there's -- do you know the building called Metalka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Only heard of it. It was not within the area of responsibility of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There were three tall buildings, you said, within your area of responsibility; is that right? Sir, I'm sorry, could you answer out loud?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There were three buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't mean to pester you, but when you nod your head the court reporter can't take it down. You just have to use words.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: There were three buildings inhabited by civilians. It is otherwise called Soping, or the yellow high-rises.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from those high-rises it is possible for snipers to shoot across the Miljacka river into the area of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. I'd like to show the witness 65 ter number 02825.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a photograph on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Look at the upper part of the photograph. There are some buildings that are red and white, white roofs, high-rise buildings. Do you recognise those buildings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You said you were stationed in Grbavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But from the Brotherhood Unity Bridge towards Strojorad and from Strojorad towards the stadium. There was no need for me to move to the right or to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you don't recognise the scene that's in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one question only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You talked about Grbavica, Witness. Can you determine the geographical location of what was close to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Within my area of responsibility or from it I could see the high school for economics, then the Bristol Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I meant the hills.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CARKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Debelo Brdo, and their sharpshooters were able to target us from there. There was Mojmilo hill as well. On the 30th of January, I was wounded from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, once again the Chamber expresses its sympathy. Your evidence has been concluded. The Chamber thanks you for coming to give it, and you may now leave. We are going to adjourn, so you will just leave with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
